fast.topic:
Week 3, taught by Abimbola Oyarinu. It runs in three strands, from first European contact to formal British occupation.

The first is the Portuguese incursion into the Niger Area. Sailors seeking new markets began exploring the West African coast in the early 15th century, improving seafaring techniques and ship design with the caravel. Portugal then dominated world trade for nearly 200 years on fabrics, spices and gold.

The incursion opened the area to the rest of the world and eventually led to colonialism and exploitation. It caused a series of wars to keep up the supply of slaves. It contributed to the abandonment of African cultures. It played a major role in the trans-Atlantic slave trade. And along the Nigerian coast it fed the growth of brass casting in Benin and the emergence of trading in the Lagos Lagoon.

The second strand is the slave trade itself. The triangular route the Portuguese developed: Africa the source, the Americas the destination, Europeans the organisers. Phillip Curtin on the largest intercontinental migration in western history, spanning 300 years. The Pope's division of the Old World, and the Spanish Asiento. The 1527 Puerto Rico uprising. The Dutch joining in the 17th century, and the British becoming biggest in the 18th.

Then the Middle Passage: 5 to 8 weeks, with each slave allotted 6ft by 1ft by 4 inches on ships of 451 to 600. Smallpox, dysentery and ophthalmia. Over 15 million reaching the Americas, and Paul Lovejoy's over 7 million dying in transit. Then the verdicts of Wole Soyinka, Walter Rodney, Washington Alcott and Claude Ake.

Abolition follows. British seizure of slave ships from 1792, with repatriation to Sierra Leone. Thomas Fowell Buxton's 1833 bill, arguing the trade had to be stopped from Africa itself.

The third strand opens with the Bight of Benin as the last slaving centre by 1840, and Lagos as the leading slave port. Beecroft's 1849 appointment is the start of direct British influence. Then the 1851 treaty with Kosoko, his refusal, and the bombardment. Akitoye's restoration on 29 December 1851, with Kosoko fleeing to Epe. Then the 1852 trade treaty, and the annexation of Lagos in 1861.

It then follows company rule. Macgregor Laird's 1857 expedition and the ports of Ado, Onitsha and Gbebe. His Central African Company of 1858, and his death in 1861. The River Niger Navigation and Trading Company of 1862. Then the amalgamation into the United African Company under Sir George Goldie-Taubman, renamed the National African Company after buying two rival French firms.

It closes with Consul Hewett's 1884 treaty-making tour and the Berlin Conference. The charter sequence of 1881, 1882 and 1886 that created the Royal Niger Company, and its control of the Niger basin by 1887. The critics Harry Johnston, Ajayi Crowther and Hoenigsberg, against the protection of Colonial Secretary Salisbury. The Oil River Protectorate of 1884 with its seven districts, renamed the Niger Coast Protectorate in 1893.

Then the decline: Sir Ralph Moor's 1891 appointment, price wars, smuggling, Joseph Chamberlain's appointment, the Brass raid on Akassa, the Kirk Commission, and the revocation of the charter.

fast.topic:
This week covers how sentences are analysed and how words are classed.

A sentence is defined as a group of words expressing a complete thought. It requires a subject (noun or pronoun) and a predicate (verb). It is analysed in two ways: by function (its purpose), and by structure (how it is built from subjects, predicates, objects, nouns and verbs).

The four structural types. Simple is one independent clause. Compound is two or more independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction such as and, but, or, so, or by a semicolon. Complex is one independent clause plus at least one dependent or subordinate clause, usually introduced by although, because, while or since. Compound-complex is two or more independent clauses plus at least one dependent clause.

The lesson gives five tips for building compound-complex sentences: relative clauses, parenthesis, context clues, punctuation (semicolon, hyphen), and details and explanations. All are in service of writing a healthy paragraph.

The four functional types are declarative (statements), imperative (commands, instructions, requests), interrogative (questions) and exclamatory (strong emotion). Conditional 'if' sentences are given as an additional fifth category, expressing a condition and its likely result.

The second half divides words into function words and content words.

Function words - also called grammatical, structure, empty or form words - carry little meaning alone. They comprise conjunctions, auxiliary or helping verbs, prepositions, articles and pronouns, plus modals, qualifiers and question words.

Content words, or lexical words, carry the main meaning. They comprise nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs.

The key discriminator to remember is stress: content words are emphasised in speech, while function words remain non-stressed. Pennebaker's figure is that function words are under one-tenth of one percent of vocabulary, but almost 60 percent of words actually used.

The third strand of the week is concord, the set of rules governing agreement between different elements in a sentence.

Subject-verb agreement is the fundamental rule, requiring the number of the subject to match the number of the verb.

The Rule of Proximity Agreement is the harder case. It requires the verb or noun to align with the closest subject when a sentence has several subject elements.

The presence of 'or' (or 'nor') in the subject decides whether the verb is singular or plural. That contrasts with 'and', which normally makes the subject plural. So students must read sentence structure carefully before choosing the verb.

fast.topic:
This week's practical studies the non-linear relationship between current and voltage in a non-ohmic resistor.

The kit is a voltmeter, an ammeter, a DC power supply, and a resistor made of either tungsten or iron, selected from a drop-down list.

After inspecting the circuit and choosing the material, the applied voltage is set from 0.1 V upwards. The Record button saves the voltmeter reading V and the current I at each step, covering the whole range up to 50 V. An Excel sheet of the data then downloads automatically.

Plotting I against V gives a curve rather than a straight line, showing that V/I is not constant and the resistor does not obey Ohm's law.

The recorded values are then used to compute I squared and the power P = IV. Plotting P against I squared gives a straight line whose gradient is the resistance, verifying Joule's law P = I squared R.

The conclusion is that current flowing through the conductor generates heat, and the resulting temperature rise changes the resistance. This is why the current-voltage response of a tungsten filament becomes non-linear at higher currents.

questions.q: Evaluate lim(x→−2) (x² + 3x − 1).
questions.concept: Limit by direct substitution
questions.why:
The expression is a polynomial, so substitute x = −2: (−2)² + 3(−2) − 1 = 4 − 6 − 1 = −3.

−11 treats (−2)² as −4; 9 loses the sign of x in the 3x term (4 + 6 − 1); 1 adds the constant instead of subtracting it (4 − 6 + 1).

questions.q: Which of these limits can be evaluated by direct substitution alone?
questions.concept: Recognising when substitution applies
questions.why:
Substitution works when it gives a well-defined expression. At x = 1, (x³ + 2)/(x² − 4) = 3/(−3) = −1: a negative denominator is a perfectly good non-zero number, so the limit is −1 by substitution.

The other three all give 0/0 at the point: (4 − 4)/(2 − 2), (3 − 3)/0 and (sin 0)/0. Each needs more work (factoring, the conjugate, L'Hôpital).

questions.q: Evaluate lim(x→3) (x² − 9)/(x − 3).
questions.concept: Limit by factoring and cancelling
questions.why:
Substitution gives 0/0, so factor: x² − 9 = (x − 3)(x + 3). Cancel the common factor (legal because x never equals 3 inside the limit) to get lim(x→3) (x + 3) = 6.

0 treats 0/0 as zero; DNE treats 0/0 as non-existence, but the form decides nothing; 3 substitutes into x alone after cancelling, forgetting the + 3.

questions.q: lim(x→c) f(x) = 4 and lim(x→c) g(x) = −2. Find lim(x→c) [3f(x) − g(x)].
questions.concept: Sum, difference and constant multiple rules
questions.why:
Split with the rules: lim [3f − g] = 3·lim f − lim g = 3(4) − (−2) = 12 + 2 = 14.

10 subtracts 2 instead of subtracting −2; 6 forgets the constant multiple 3 (4 + 2); −24 multiplies 3, 4 and −2 as if the rule were a product.

questions.q: Evaluate lim(x→1) (2x + 1)³.
questions.concept: Limit of a power
questions.why:
Take the limit first, then the power: [lim(x→1) (2x + 1)]³ = (2 + 1)³ = 3³ = 27.

9 multiplies 3 by the exponent instead of cubing; 3 takes the limit and forgets the cube; 8 cubes the 2x and drops the + 1.

questions.q: Evaluate lim(x→3) (2x²)/(5x).
questions.concept: Limit of a quotient
questions.why:
The limit of the denominator is 15 ≠ 0, so the quotient rule applies: [lim 2x²]/[lim 5x] = 2(9)/(5·3) = 18/15 = 6/5.

18/5 forgets the x in the denominator; 2/5 cancels x² against x completely instead of leaving one x; 90 multiplies 18 by 5 instead of dividing.

questions.q: If 4 − x² ≤ f(x) ≤ 4 + x² for all x, find lim(x→0) f(x).
options: Cannot be found without knowing f
questions.concept: Squeeze Theorem
questions.why:
Both bounds have the same limit at 0: lim (4 − x²) = 4 and lim (4 + x²) = 4. f is trapped between them, so by the Squeeze Theorem lim(x→0) f(x) = 4.

0 takes the limit of x² alone; 8 adds the two bounds; 'cannot be found' misses the point of the theorem, which gives the limit without a formula for f.

questions.q: Direct substitution in lim(x→5) (x² − 25)/(x − 5) gives 0/0. Which conclusion is correct?
options: The limit may still exist; more algebra is needed
questions.concept: Meaning of the indeterminate form 0/0
questions.why:
0/0 is indeterminate: the form itself decides nothing, so you must do more algebra. Here factoring gives lim (x + 5) = 10, a perfectly good limit.

'The limit is 0' treats 0/0 as ordinary division into zero; 'the limit is 1' treats any number over itself as 1; 'does not exist' confuses the function being undefined at 5 with the limit failing.

questions.q: Evaluate lim(x→0) (eˣ − 1)/x by L'Hôpital's Rule. Which quotient f′(x)/g′(x) do you evaluate, and what is the limit?
options: eˣ/x, so the limit does not exist
questions.concept: L'Hôpital's Rule, first application
questions.why:
Substituting x = 0 gives (1 − 1)/0 = 0/0, an indeterminate form, so the rule is allowed. Take f(x) = eˣ − 1 and g(x) = x separately, so f′(x) = eˣ and g′(x) = 1, and the new quotient is eˣ/1, whose value at 0 is e⁰ = 1.

eˣ/x differentiates only the numerator, (xeˣ − eˣ + 1)/x² applies the quotient rule instead of the rule itself, and reading e⁰ as 0 gives the limit 0.

questions.q: Evaluate lim(x→5) 1/x² and 1/[lim(x→5) x²] separately. What is the value they share?
questions.concept: Verifying the reciprocal property
questions.why:
Direct substitution on the left gives 1/5² = 1/25. On the right, lim(x→5) x² = 25 first, and then the reciprocal is 1/25. Both sides come to 1/25, or 0.04, which is what the reciprocal property predicts, and it is valid here because lim x² = 25 is not zero.

25 forgets to take the reciprocal at all, 1/5 forgets to square, and 1/10 comes from differentiating x² instead of substituting into it.

questions.q: Evaluate lim(x→0) (√(x + 1) − 1)/x.
questions.concept: Limit by multiplying by the conjugate
questions.why:
Substitution gives (1 − 1)/0 = 0/0, so multiply top and bottom by the conjugate √(x + 1) + 1. The numerator collapses to (x + 1) − 1 = x, leaving x/[x(√(x + 1) + 1)], and cancelling x gives 1/(√(x + 1) + 1), which at x = 0 is 1/(1 + 1) = 1/2.

1 comes from forgetting the + 1 left in the denominator, 0 comes from reading 0/0 as zero, and 2 inverts the final fraction.

questions.q: In lim(x→2) (x² − 4)/(x − 2) the factor (x − 2) is cancelled even though x − 2 = 0 at x = 2. Why is that cancellation legitimate?
options: The form 0/0 equals 1, so the two copies of the factor cancel
Cancelling a common factor is allowed in any fraction, zero or not
After cancelling, the function is defined at x = 2, so the hole closes
x only approaches 2 and never equals it, so x − 2 is close to zero but never zero
questions.concept: Why cancelling a common factor inside a limit is legitimate
questions.why:
Inside a limit x runs towards 2 without ever arriving, so x − 2 is a small nonzero number throughout and dividing by it is legal. Once cancelled, the expression equals x + 2 at every x except 2 itself, and a limit only inspects nearby values, so lim(x→2) (x + 2) = 4 even though f(2) is undefined.

0/0 is not 1, cancelling a genuinely zero factor is not allowed, and cancelling does not change the original function's domain.

questions.q: A cell of emf 9.0 V and internal resistance 0.50 Ω delivers a current of 2.0 A to a circuit. What is the terminal potential difference?
questions.concept: Terminal p.d. from V = ε − Ir
questions.why:
The lost volts inside the cell are Ir = 2.0 × 0.50 = 1.0 V, so V = ε − Ir = 9.0 − 1.0 = 8.0 V.

10 V adds the lost volts instead of subtracting them; 9.0 V ignores the internal resistance, which is only right when no current flows; 1.0 V is the lost volts themselves, not the terminal p.d.

questions.q: A metal rod 0.40 m long moves at 5.0 m/s at right angles to a uniform magnetic field of 0.25 T, the field being perpendicular to the rod. What emf is induced across the rod?
questions.concept: Motional emf ε = Bvl
questions.why:
ε = Bvl = 0.25 × 5.0 × 0.40 = 0.50 V.

0.10 V is Bl and forgets the speed; 1.25 V is Bv and forgets the length; 2.0 V is vl and forgets the field.

questions.q: The magnetic flux through each turn of a 100-turn coil changes by 6.0 × 10⁻³ Wb in 0.020 s. What is the magnitude of the induced emf?
questions.concept: Faraday's law with N turns
questions.why:
|ε| = N ΔΦ/Δt = 100 × 6.0 × 10⁻³/0.020 = 100 × 0.30 = 30 V.

0.30 V is the emf per turn, forgetting N; 3.0 V is a power-of-ten slip in 6.0 × 10⁻³/0.020; 0.12 V multiplies by the time instead of dividing by it.

questions.q: A 4.0 μF capacitor is charged to 50 V. How much energy does it store?
questions.concept: Energy stored in a capacitor, U = ½CV²
questions.why:
U = ½CV² = ½ × 4.0 × 10⁻⁶ × (50)² = ½ × 4.0 × 10⁻⁶ × 2500 = 5.0 × 10⁻³ J.

1.0 × 10⁻² J leaves out the ½ (that is QV, the work at constant voltage); 5.0 × 10³ J drops the μ prefix; 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ J uses V instead of V².

questions.q: In vacuum the electric field in a region is 2.0 × 10⁴ N/C. Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F/m. What is the energy stored per unit volume in that region?
questions.concept: Energy density of an electric field
questions.why:
u = ½ε₀E² = ½ × 8.85 × 10⁻¹² × (2.0 × 10⁴)² = ½ × 8.85 × 10⁻¹² × 4.0 × 10⁸ = 1.77 × 10⁻³ J/m³.

8.85 × 10⁻⁸ uses E instead of E²; 3.54 × 10⁻³ leaves out the ½; '1.77 × 10⁻³ J' has the right number with the wrong unit, since ½ε₀E² is energy per cubic metre and must be multiplied by a volume to give joules.

questions.q: A parallel-plate capacitor in vacuum has plates of area 0.050 m² separated by 1.0 mm. Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F/m. What is its capacitance?
questions.concept: Parallel-plate capacitance C = ε₀A/d
questions.why:
Convert d = 1.0 mm = 1.0 × 10⁻³ m. C = ε₀A/d = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² × 0.050/1.0 × 10⁻³ = 4.4 × 10⁻¹⁰ F (0.44 nF).

4.4 × 10⁻¹³ F leaves d as 1.0 (millimetres not converted); 1.8 × 10⁻¹³ F swaps A and d; 4.4 × 10⁻⁷ F treats mm as 10⁻⁶ m.

questions.q: A capacitor measures 20 pF with vacuum between its plates and 70 pF when the gap is completely filled with an insulating oil. What is the dielectric constant of the oil?
questions.concept: Dielectric constant from the change in capacitance
questions.why:
A dielectric multiplies the capacitance by K, so K = C/C₀ = 70/20 = 3.5. K has no unit and is always above 1 for a real material.

50 subtracts the capacitances instead of dividing; 0.29 divides the wrong way round (a K below 1 is impossible); 90 adds them.

questions.q: A dry cell is marked '1.5 V'. Which statement says what this emf means?
options: The cell gives 1.5 J of energy to each coulomb it drives round the circuit
The cell pushes each coulomb with a force of 1.5 N
The terminals are always 1.5 V apart, whatever current flows
The cell delivers 1.5 W to the circuit
questions.concept: Meaning of emf as energy per unit charge
questions.why:
Emf is work done per unit charge, ε = W/Q, so 1 V = 1 J/C: the cell converts 1.5 J of chemical energy for every coulomb it drives round. It is not a force despite its name.

'1.5 N' confuses the volt with the newton; 'always 1.5 V apart' describes the terminal p.d., which falls below ε by Ir as soon as current flows; watts measure power, not energy per charge.

questions.q: A 15 μF capacitor carries a charge of 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ C. What are the potential difference across it and the energy it stores?
questions.concept: Potential difference and energy from the charge on a capacitor
questions.why:
V = Q/C = 3.0 × 10⁻⁴/15 × 10⁻⁶ = 20 V. Then U = ½QV = ½(3.0 × 10⁻⁴)(20) = 3.0 × 10⁻³ J, the same as Q²/2C = 9.0 × 10⁻⁸/3.0 × 10⁻⁵.

6.0 × 10⁻³ J leaves out the factor ½; 1.5 × 10⁻⁴ J uses ½CV instead of ½CV²; the last option multiplies Q by C instead of dividing.

questions.q: Emf is defined as work done per unit charge. What is its dimensional formula?
questions.concept: Dimensional formula of emf
questions.why:
Work = force × displacement = [M][L T⁻²][L] = [M L² T⁻²], and charge = current × time = [I T]. Dividing, emf = [M L² T⁻²]/[I T] = [M L² T⁻³ I⁻¹].

[M L² T⁻² I⁻¹] forgets the T that comes with the charge; [M L T⁻³ I⁻¹] uses force in place of work; [M L² T⁻¹ I] multiplies by the charge instead of dividing.

questions.q: The insulating film in a capacitor has a dielectric strength of 3.0 × 10⁶ V/m and a thickness of 0.20 mm. What is the largest potential difference it can hold before the dielectric breaks down?
questions.concept: Breakdown potential from dielectric strength
questions.why:
Between parallel plates V = Ed, and the largest field the film tolerates is its dielectric strength, so V_max = (3.0 × 10⁶)(0.20 × 10⁻³) = 6.0 × 10² V = 600 V.

6.0 × 10⁵ V leaves the thickness in millimetres; 6.0 × 10⁴ V reads 0.20 mm as 0.020 m; 1.5 × 10¹⁰ divides by the thickness instead of multiplying.

questions.q: A metal plate and a slab of glass are each placed in a steady external electric field. Why is the field inside the metal zero at equilibrium while the field inside the glass is reduced but not zero?
options: The metal has no electrons free to make a field inside it, while glass has electrons that make one
The metal's free electrons are used up cancelling the field; glass holds fewer electrons, so less is cancelled
The metal reflects the field at its surface, while glass transmits part of it and absorbs the rest
Free electrons in the metal redistribute until they cancel the field; glass has bound electrons that only polarise, cutting it by K
questions.concept: Field inside a conductor versus inside a dielectric
questions.why:
In a conductor the electrons are free, so they keep moving until the surface charge they build up produces a field that exactly cancels the applied one; any leftover field would move more charge, so equilibrium means zero field inside. In glass the electrons are bound to their atoms and can only shift slightly, so the polarisation produces an opposing field that reduces the applied field by the factor K but can never cancel it.

The other options either deny the metal its free electrons, treat electrons as a supply that runs out, or describe optics rather than electrostatics.
